title: How The Hum Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore "the Hum," a low-frequency droning sound that some people (roughly two percent of local populations, often in rural, Western, European-ancestry areas) say they hear, often at night and indoors, while others cannot. They cover the named hums around the world (Taos Hum, Bristol Hum, Auckland Hum, Windsor Hum), Glenn McPherson's World Hum Map and Database, David Deming's 2004 study, theories involving VLF/ELF radio waves and the US Navy TACAMO and HAARP programs, tinnitus and hyperacusis as explanations, the Windsor hum traced to the Zug Island steel plant, habituation and sensitization, the claimed link to violence (Adam Lanza, Aaron Alexis), and the Portuguese OGMA aircraft plant epilepsy and low-frequency noise health investigation. The episode closes with listener mail about a limousine cattle ranch in South Dakota.

segments.title: Opening banter and vocal fry
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, including a flubbed show intro and a tangent on vocal fry, and note that people who hear the hum tend to focus on it more with exposure.

segments.title: What the Hum is
segments.summary: The hosts define the Hum as a low-frequency drone heard by about two percent of local populations, often at night, indoors, and in rural areas. Named hums include the Auckland, Bristol and Taos hums, and it has been described since the 1800s, with modern descriptions from the 1950s to 1970s.

segments.title: World Hum Map and geographic concentration
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the hum's concentration in Western and European-ancestry countries and the World Hum Map and Database run by Glenn McPherson, which plots reports from people who fill out a questionnaire. They note the English-language bias of the database as one possible explanation.

segments.title: Tinnitus, mental health and David Deming's study
segments.summary: A physician's view of hum sufferers' symptoms leads to two explanations, tinnitus or mental strain. David Deming, a University of Oklahoma geoscientist, wrote a 2004 study that explains these away and discusses other theories.

segments.title: VLF and ELF radio waves and electromagnetic sound
segments.summary: The hosts explain VLF and ELF radio frequencies and the theory that these tones drive people crazy. They discuss whether electromagnetic waves can be perceived as sound, the ESA Comet 67P clicking sound, and the debate over whether the hum is electromagnetic or acoustic.

segments.title: Windsor hum, Zug Island, and Taos investigation
segments.summary: Canadian researcher Colin Novak spent a year studying the Windsor Hum and traced it to a steel plant on Zug Island in Michigan, which was reportedly curtailed. The Taos Hum prompted investigation by the University of New Mexico and Sandia Labs. The hosts mention the X-Files episode Drive.

segments.title: Age, hearing and government programs
segments.summary: The hosts discuss age-related hearing loss, with low-frequency hearing being relatively preserved around age fifty, and the theory that some people are more sensitive to low frequencies. They cover US military programs HAARP and TACAMO, and Deming's view that TACAMO may be a source, along with the tinfoil hat idea.

segments.title: Habituation and sensitization
segments.summary: Chuck describes his night job with buzzing fluorescent lights to explain habituation, and the hosts explain sensitization as a possible reason hum sufferers cannot tune out the sound.
